Welcome toShearing a Gas

Slide one plate past another through air — how does the drag depend on pressure?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: momentum carried across a plane in a sheared gas, and how the drag on the plates depends on pressure and gap

Source

Concept
Kinetic-theory viscosity: molecules crossing a plane at x₀ carry the drift momentum of the place of their last collision, a perpendicular distance 2λ/3 away. Air at 300 K (m = 29 u, d = 0.37 nm, σ = πd²) fills a gap L between a fixed plate and one sliding at u₀ = 1 m/s.
Serves
Explaining how the drag on the moving plate depends on pressure and gap width, in terms of the crossing rate J and the drift-speed difference Δu each crosser brings.
Inquiry
Five questions to answer and then check in the sim: sweep the pressure decade by decade with the 1 mm gap (the decade chips under the slider land on each decade exactly), read the drag, J, Δu and λ as each question asks, then compare gap widths at high and low pressure. A summary card closes the set.
Misconception
Addressed through the answer choices; each choice has its own feedback, shown after a choice is made.
Readouts
In the sidebar Readouts panel: pressure p and mean free path λ; J, the number of molecules crossing the plane x₀ in each direction per square metre per second; Δu, the drift-speed difference each crosser brings; and the drag τ = J m Δu. Here τ is the drag per unit area on the plate, a shear stress; it is not the mean time between collisions, which the notes (§1.3) also call τ.
Model
Computed, not simulated molecule by molecule: n = p/(kBT), v̄ = √(8kBT/(πm)), λ = 1/(√2 nσ), η = (1/3) n m v̄ λ, uy(x) = u₀(x + 2λ/3)/(L + 4λ/3), τ = η u₀/(L + 4λ/3), J = (1/4) n v̄, Δu = (4λ/3)u₀/(L + 4λ/3), τ = J m Δu. The lecture treats λ ≪ L and λ ≫ L; this formula is the simplest one that reproduces both limits. The gap is always drawn at the same screen width, so the horizontal scale changes with L; u₀ is drawn as 70 % of the gap height. The simple (1/3) n m v̄ λ formula gives η = 1.24 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s for this air, about two thirds of the measured 1.85 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s; a full Chapman–Enskog treatment closes the gap, and the pressure and gap dependence is unchanged.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honors it
Commit, then checkEach question is gated on a committed answer; the chart holds only the points the student has visited, so no curve is shown in advance. Free Exploration opens with the 1 mm curve already drawn.
Readout disciplineThe Readouts panel in the sidebar shows only the one or two quantities the open question uses; all five appear in free exploration.
Operational quantitiesp, λ, J, Δu and τ are live SI readouts computed from the same formulas as the drawing, and τ = J m Δu holds for every setting.
Honest geometryThe 2λ/3 brackets are drawn to the gap's horizontal scale, are not drawn when narrower than 3 px, and stop at the plates when 2λ/3 exceeds L/2.
Discovery not labellingNo line, label or shading marks where λ equals L or where the drag changes behaviour.
Comparison on one scalePoints from the previous gap stay on the same fixed log axes in grey while a new set builds, so the two gaps are compared directly.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Thinning a dense gas

Keep the 1 mm gap and start at 100 kPa, where the drag reads 12.35 mPa. Lower the pressure one decade at a time to 1 kPa, watching the drag readout and the chart. What happens to the drag as the gas is thinned a hundredfold?

2 · What makes up the loss

Return to 100 kPa with the 1 mm gap and lower the pressure to 1 kPa again, this time watching the crossing rate J, which falls a hundredfold from 2.82 × 10²⁷ to 2.82 × 10²⁵ m⁻² s⁻¹, and the other readouts. What makes up for the hundredfold fall in the number of molecules crossing the plane in each direction?

3 · Below 1 kPa

Keep the 1 mm gap and continue lowering the pressure from 1 kPa, one decade at a time, down to 0.1 Pa, watching the chart and the 2λ/3 brackets. What does the drag do?

4 · Longer than the gap

Stay at 0.1 Pa with the 1 mm gap, where λ reads 68.1 mm, and look at the drift arrows, the brackets, which now end on the plates, and the readout Δu = 0.989 m/s. Why does the drag fall with the pressure once the mean free path is longer than the gap?

5 · Widening the gap

Set the pressure to 100 kPa with the 1 mm gap, read the drag, and switch the gap to 10 mm. Then set the pressure to 0.1 Pa and switch the gap between 1 mm and 10 mm again. What does widening the gap do to the drag at the two pressures?

6 · Momentum carried across a gas

Viscosity comes from molecules carrying drift momentum across a plane from where they last collided, 2λ/3 away.

In a dense gas, thinning it changes nothing: fewer molecules cross, but each brings a larger Δu, so η = (1/3) n m v̄ λ does not depend on the pressure and the drag is η u₀/L. Maxwell confirmed this for air in 1866.

Once λ is longer than the gap, the plates cap Δu at u₀ and the drag falls in proportion to the pressure, whatever the gap. Spinning-rotor vacuum gauges use this to measure low pressures.

The Physics

Shearing a Gas between Two Plates · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Air fills the gap L between two parallel plates. One plate is fixed and the other slides past it at u0 = 1 m/s. The air is at 300 K, with molecular mass 29 u and diameter 0.37 nm. The sim reports the drag τ, the force per unit area the air exerts on the sliding plate, and lets you set the pressure p and the gap.

What you'll learn

  • How the drag τ is built from the crossing rate J and the drift difference Δu.
  • How τ depends on the pressure p.
  • How τ depends on the gap width L.
The setup. The plane x0 is the plane whose crossings the sim counts. The gas between the plates is drawn as dots.

What's on screen

  • Blue arrows: the drift velocity uy(x) of the gas across the gap. The dashed blue line joins their tips.
  • Dashed plane: x0, labelled 2λ/3. The drag is worked out from the molecules that cross it.
  • Chart dots: τ against p, both on log scales, for the gap you have set. The cyan dot is your current setting.
  • Readouts: p, the mean free path λ, the crossing rate J, Δu and the drag τ = J m Δu.
See itStart from the opening picture, with your current settings. Watch for: the drift arrows, the plane x0, and the readouts p, λ, J, Δu and τ.

Fixed: air at T = 300 K, m = 29 u, d = 0.37 nm, σ = πd2, u0 = 1 m/s, so the mean speed is v = 468.0 m/s. The τ in this sim is the drag per unit area, not the time between collisions of notes §1.3.

03

A crossing molecule brings the drift of its last collision, 2λ/3 away

Molecules cross the plane x0 in both directions. Each carries the drift uy of the place where it last collided, a distance ℓ = 2λ/3 back along x (notes 1.38). Per unit area ¼ n v molecules cross each way every second, so equation (1.36), with uy in the place of χ, gives the momentum passed across:

τ = J m Δu,    J = ¼ n v

J is the crossing rate each way and Δu = uy(x0 + ℓ) − uy(x0 − ℓ) is the drift difference a crosser brings.
The detail at the plane x0, as in notes Fig. 8. The arrows are the drift at the two last-collision places.

The drift runs from 0 to u0 between points ℓ behind each plate, so its gradient is u0/(L + 4λ/3), and Δu is 2ℓ times that:

Δu = (4λ/3) u0 / (L + 4λ/3)

At the opening, 100 kPa and 1 mm: λ = 68.1 nm, J = 2.82 × 1027 m−2 s−1, Δu = 9.08 × 10−5 m/s, τ = 12.35 mPa.
See itLook at the opening setting, 100 kPa and a 1 mm gap. Watch for: the dashed plane x0, its 2λ/3 label, and J, Δu and τ in the readouts.
04

Thinning a dense gas leaves the drag unchanged

While λ is far smaller than L, L + 4λ/3 ≈ L and Δu ≈ (4λ/3) u0/L. Now J ∝ n ∝ p and Δu ∝ λ ∝ 1/p, so J rises by the factor that Δu falls by, and J m Δu does not change:

τ = ⅓ n m v λ · u0/L = η u0/L

Notes (1.40)–(1.42), with η = m v/(3√2 σ) (1.47): no n or p is left in it.

In the sim η = 1.235 × 10−5 Pa s, so ηu0/L = 12.35 mPa for the 1 mm gap. From 100 kPa to 1 kPa, J falls from 2.82 × 1027 to 2.82 × 1025 m−2 s−1 and Δu grows from 9.08 × 10−5 to 9.00 × 10−3 m/s. The drag goes from 12.35 to 12.24 mPa, a change of under 1%.

J, Δu and τ for the 1 mm gap, each divided by its value at 100 kPa. Between 1 and 100 kPa J and Δu mirror each other and τ is level.
See itLower the pressure from 100 kPa to 1 kPa in steps of one decade. Watch for: J falling and Δu rising by the same factor, while τ barely moves.
05

Past the gap width, the mean free path no longer helps and the drag falls with p

At 0.1 Pa, λ = 68.1 mm, about 68 gaps. A molecule now crosses from plate to plate with no collision in between, so Δu = 0.989 m/s and cannot pass u0 = 1 m/s. The sim draws the brackets as L/2, ending on the plates, because 2λ/3 would be longer than half the gap.

The drift across the 1 mm gap, from the sim's profile. Open circles: the plate speeds. Filled circles: the gas next to each plate, in m/s.

J still falls in proportion to p, but Δu has nothing left to give, so τ falls with it: 11.32 mPa at 100 Pa, 6.47 at 10 Pa, 1.225 at 1 Pa and 0.1345 at 0.1 Pa. The last decade cuts it 9.1-fold. The limit is ¼ n v m u0, a crosser from each plate passing on all of u0: 0.1360 mPa at 0.1 Pa, and the notes' problem 4 for §1.4.

See itLower the pressure in decades from 1 kPa to 0.1 Pa. Watch for: the brackets growing to the plates, Δu approaching 1 m/s, and τ falling on the chart.
06

Widening the gap cuts the drag tenfold in a dense gas and hardly at all in a thin one

In a dense gas τ = ηu0/L, so ten times the gap gives a tenth of the drag. At 100 kPa the gaps 0.1, 1 and 10 mm give 123.4, 12.35 and 1.235 mPa (notes, problem 3 of §1.4). At 0.1 Pa the same gaps give 0.1359, 0.1345 and 0.1225 mPa: Δu is already near u0 for each (0.999, 0.989, 0.901), so the drag stays near ¼ n v m u0 whatever L is.

τ against p for the three gaps. The circles mark the half-drag points, 90.8, 9.08 and 0.908 Pa.

The curves part where 4λ/3 reaches L, and there τ has fallen to half of ηu0/L. For the 1 mm gap that is at 9.08 Pa. A gap ten times narrower puts it ten times higher.

See itAt 100 kPa switch between the three gaps, then do the same at 0.1 Pa. Watch for: the drag changing tenfold per gap step at 100 kPa and hardly changing at 0.1 Pa.
07

Where it matters

  • Pressure-independent viscosity. Maxwell predicted in the 1860s that the viscosity of a gas does not depend on its pressure, and tested it. The notes call it good evidence for the kinetic picture, since nothing in the behaviour of liquids would suggest it.
  • Vacuum insulation. When λ exceeds the size of the container, momentum and energy go straight from wall to wall and the viscosity and thermal conductivity become proportional to p. That is what makes a vacuum flask work.
Go deeper: how far to trust the numbers

The sim's η = 1.235 × 10−5 Pa s is about two thirds of the measured 1.85 × 10−5 Pa s for air, as the sim's own information panel says. The notes warn that the numerical factors of this argument are rough, while its dependence on p and L is sound. They give the two limits, ηu0/L and about ¼ n v m u0. The sim joins them with the single formula τ = ηu0/(L + 4λ/3).

08

Summary

In one line. The drag is a crossing rate times the momentum each crosser brings, and the sim lets you change both through p and L.

Key points

  • τ = J m Δu, with J = ¼ n v and Δu = (4λ/3)u0/(L + 4λ/3).
  • λ << L: τ = ηu0/L. It does not depend on p and goes as 1/L.
  • λ >> L: Δu → u0 and τ ≈ ¼ n v m u0. It goes as p and hardly depends on L.
  • τ is half of ηu0/L where 4λ/3 = L.

Common mix-ups

  • “A thinner gas always drags less.” Not while λ fits in the gap: 12.35 mPa at 100 kPa and 12.24 at 1 kPa.
  • “The drag always goes as 1/L.” Only for a dense gas. At 0.1 Pa it is 0.1359 mPa for 0.1 mm and 0.1225 for 10 mm.
  • “The drag reaches zero at some pressure.” It falls in proportion to p, to 0.1345 mPa at 0.1 Pa.

Things to try on your own

  • At 100 kPa read τ for each gap and multiply by L: the product is the same, 12.35 mPa mm.
  • For the 1 mm gap, find the pressure step at which τ first reads below half of 12.35 mPa (7.94 Pa, just past 9.08 Pa).
